column1: What is the canonical standard form of a constrained optimization problem?
column2: Minimize $f(x)$ subject to $h_i(x) = 0$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$ (equality constraints) and $g_j(x) \le 0$ for $j=1,\ldots,p$ (inequality constraints), over $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

column1: Why does convexity matter so much in optimization theory?
column2: Convexity guarantees that any local minimum is a global minimum, gradient-based algorithms converge reliably, and strong duality theory yields tractable computational methods.

column1: What are the first-order and second-order necessary/sufficient conditions for an unconstrained local minimizer $x^*$?
column2:
Necessary: $
abla f(x^*) = 0$ (stationarity). Sufficient (with stationarity): $
abla^2 f(x^*)$ is positive definite. If $
abla f(x^*) 
eq 0$, descent direction $p = -
abla f(x^*)$ exists; if the Hessian has a negative eigenvalue, a descent direction along that eigenvector exists.

column1: Define the generic iterative update rule for descent methods and distinguish first-order from second-order methods.
column2: $x_{k+1} = x_k + \alpha_k p_k$, where $\alpha_k$ is the step size and $p_k$ is the search direction. First-order methods (gradient descent, conjugate gradient) use only gradient information; second-order methods (Newton's method, quasi-Newton) incorporate Hessian (curvature) information.

column1: State the full KKT (Karush-Kuhn-Tucker) conditions for a constrained NLP minimum $x^*$.
column2:
Stationarity: $
abla f(x^*) + \sum_i \lambda_i^* 
abla h_i(x^*) + \sum_j \mu_j^* 
abla g_j(x^*) = 0$. Primal feasibility: $h_i(x^*)=0$, $g_j(x^*)\le 0$. Dual feasibility: $\mu_j^* \ge 0$. Complementary slackness: $\mu_j^* g_j(x^*) = 0$ for all $j$.

column1: What does complementary slackness ($\mu_j^* g_j(x^*) = 0$) mean economically?
column2: An inequality constraint only exerts first-order force on the optimum if it is active ($g_j(x^*)=0$, positive shadow price $\mu_j^* > 0$); a slack (inactive) constraint ($g_j(x^*) < 0$) must have zero multiplier $\mu_j^* = 0$.

column1: What is the active set $\mathcal{A}(x^*)$ in constrained optimization?
column2: The set of inequality constraints that hold with equality at $x^*$: $\mathcal{A}(x^*) = \{j : g_j(x^*) = 0\}$.

column1: What distinguishes linear programs, quadratic programs, and convex programs in the optimization taxonomy?
column2: Linear programs: affine objective and constraints. Quadratic programs: quadratic objective term with linear constraints. Convex programs: arbitrary convex objective over a convex constraint set, preserving the local-equals-global-minimum guarantee.

column1: Why does integer programming become NP-hard while linear programming remains polynomial-time solvable?
column2: Imposing integrality constraints ($x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$) destroys the polyhedral/convexity structure exploited by LP algorithms (Simplex, Ellipsoid, Interior-Point); even deciding feasibility of a single integer solution becomes NP-complete.

column1: What are the three strategic approaches to tackling NP-hard discrete optimization problems?
column2: 1) Exact methods (branch-and-bound, cutting planes) that prune the exponential search space. 2) Dynamic programming, achieving polynomial time when optimal substructure exists. 3) Approximation/heuristic methods that trade optimality guarantees for tractability.

column1: In simulated annealing, what role does the temperature schedule $T(t)$ play, and what is the Boltzmann acceptance distribution?
column2: $T(t)$ controls the probability of accepting worse solutions to escape local minima, typically cooling via $T(t) = c/\log(1+t)$. The target stationary distribution is $\pi(x) \propto \exp(-f(x)/T)$, guaranteeing convergence to the global optimum as $T \to 0$ sufficiently slowly.

column1: What is the core principle enabling Benders and Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition for large-scale structured optimization?
column2: Exploiting block-angular/block-diagonal problem structure and strong duality: a master problem proposes decisions while subproblems validate feasibility/optimality via dual certificates (cuts), iteratively refining the master problem.
